Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette:
Esperanza is a 74-year-old Latin American woman who has worked as a pharmacist for nearly four decades, a career she built with quiet discipline and a deep sense of purpose. She is married - her second marriage, to a man she describes as gentle - and she came to the intake appointment dressed neatly, speaking in measured sentences that occasionally broke apart when she reached certain words. Her PCL-5 score of 66 places her in the severe range, and the picture that emerged across the first several sessions is one of a woman whose interior life has been reshaped, almost architecturally, by years of physical abuse at the hands of her first husband.

The abuse spanned nearly a decade. What Esperanza returns to most often is not a continuous narrative but a series of frozen images: herself pressed against the kitchen wall, his hand raised; the particular angle of light through a window the moment a door slammed open and she knew what was coming; the sound of footsteps in the hallway, the specific creak of a hinge. She describes remembering the events not as a story she can tell from beginning to end but as a handful of vivid stills, each one complete and unbearable - a snapshot quality that means the past never quite recedes into sequence. More distressing still, when these images surface, she does not only see them. She feels her shoulders curl inward, her arms draw up, her body returning without her permission to the posture of someone bracing for a blow. The memories carry a physical signature that belongs to then but arrives in now, and when they come, her body floods with shame - not anger at what was done to her, but a deep, mortifying sense that she allowed it, that she was the kind of woman to whom such things happened.

It is this shame, and the beliefs it has calcified into, that now organise so much of Esperanza's daily life. She has come to believe she is no longer the competent, capable woman who counselled patients for decades; that person, she feels, would not have endured what she endured. She has lost whatever faith she once held in people and in the order of things. The belief in her own weakness had also, over time, expanded the territory of what felt dangerous: once she had accepted that she was the kind of woman to whom terrible things happened, almost any sign of closeness or unpredictability became a potential signal - a coworker's unexpected warmth, a door opening in a room where she had not expected anyone to be. Most corrosively, she has settled into a conviction that she is simply weak - and it is this belief that makes her most afraid of what other people might see if they got close enough to look. The conviction of weakness did not stay still; it kept pulling the memories forward, as though they were proof she needed to keep consulting - she would find herself back against the kitchen wall not only when something in the world summoned her there, but when the thought arrived on its own: you let this happen, and here is what it looked like. The appraisal of weakness functions almost as a standing instruction: do not let anyone near enough to confirm it. So she avoids people, deflecting invitations from colleagues at the pharmacy where she still works part-time, keeping conversations transactional. When a patient lingers to chat, or a coworker asks how she is doing with the warmth of someone who genuinely wants to know, Esperanza feels the approach as a kind of exposure and steps back - literally, sometimes, moving behind the dispensing counter. The belief in her own weakness also makes her afraid of her own emotional interior; she suppresses strong feeling with the vigilance of someone managing a hazardous substance, and she has learned not to look at herself in mirrors or to attend to her body in any deliberate way, because her body still feels like the site of her humiliation.

These avoidances, which seemed at first like reasonable self-protection, have over time reinforced the very beliefs they were meant to shield her from. Because she never allows herself to feel, she has no evidence that she could survive feeling. Because she keeps people at a distance, she has no experience of being known and not found wanting. The isolation has made the pharmacy feel smaller; she has reduced her hours twice in the past year, telling her husband it is because of her age. The avoidance had also drawn its own map around her: each room she slipped out of, each conversation she cut short, each shift she no longer worked had become a landmark she could not pass without the thought arriving - another place, another person, another ordinary thing that was no longer safe.

The threat system that was shaped during the abuse has never fully deactivated. Inside her own home - the home she shares with a kind man - Esperanza listens for the sound of doors. When one opens or slams, her body goes rigid before her mind catches up, and the alarm her nervous system sounds pulls a memory forward, which sharpens the sense of danger, which makes her scan for the next sound. Living inside that alarm, day after day, had become its own kind of evidence: feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering - that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe, that the vigilance was not a symptom but simply an accurate reading of who she had become. A comment from her husband about family - her children from her first marriage, her estrangement from a sister - lands as a trigger because the family she came from is woven into the history of what happened to her, and the mention of it can collapse the distance between then and now in an instant. Someone moving toward her emotionally produces the same collapse: closeness itself has become a warning signal. And each time a trigger fires - the creak of a hinge, a hand extended across a counter, a reference to her children - the conclusion arrives with it, quiet and certain: this is what weakness looks like, this flinching, this inability to simply be present in an ordinary moment.

What finally brought Esperanza to seek help was a moment at the pharmacy three months ago. A patient - an elderly woman, frightened, asking questions about a new medication - reached across the counter and briefly touched Esperanza's hand. Esperanza froze, then excused herself to the back room, where she sat for twenty minutes unable to move. She told no one. But that evening she told her husband she thought something was wrong with her, and he found her the referral. What she is most afraid of, she said at the end of the first session, is that she is too old and too far gone for anything to change. What she is hoping for, said more quietly, is to feel like herself again - though she is no longer entirely sure who that was.

violations.explanation: Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph establishes that triggering stimuli (e.g., sounds, touch, family mentions) causally lead to or activate Esperanza's negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs about weakness or shame); triggers are linked to memory and threat but not directly to negative appraisals.

Negative Appraisals → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Esperanza's negative appraisals (e.g., belief in her own weakness) causally sensitise or generate triggering stimuli; the beliefs drive avoidance but are not described as expanding or creating the set of triggers.

Negative Appraisals → Memory: No paragraph conveys that Esperanza's negative appraisals (e.g., shame, belief in weakness) causally bring forward or activate her intrusive memories; memories are described as arising from triggers and threat cues, but not from the appraisals themselves.

Threat → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph establishes that the activated threat/alarm state causally produces or reinforces Esperanza's negative appraisals; the threat system is described as pulling memories forward and driving scanning behaviour, but is not linked to generating the beliefs about weakness or shame.

Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that Esperanza's avoidance behaviours or safety behaviours causally create or expand her triggering stimuli; the vignette notes avoidance reinforces beliefs but does not describe it as producing new or broader triggers.
